newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE-UK debates mix of human rights and foreign policy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-UK debates mix of human rights and foreign policy.

text.p: Britain's new Foreign Secretary Robin Cook could well end up cursing the day he stood up and announced to the world that British foreign policy would revolve around human rights.

Cook, fulfilling a pledge made in the run-up to Labour's crushing election win on May 1, appears to have set a collision course with several powerful states by saying Britain could not ignore the human rights record of its trading partners.

"Our foreign policy must have an ethical dimension and must support the demands of other peoples for the democratic rights on which we insist for ourselves," he said recently, singling out Nigeria for special attention.

But as U.S. and Canadian leaders have found out to their cost, personal attacks and humiliation can lie in store for those who seek election on a strongly pro-human rights ticket and are then forced to weaken their stance.
Cook's quandary is how to balance his desire for improved human rights abroad with the interests of Britain's immensely powerful arms industry, which employs a total of 400,000 people.
LUCRATIVE TRADE TARGETS BAD ON RIGHTS
Activists in Britain have long criticised the human rights record of countries like China, Saudi Arabia and Indonesia, which also happen to be juicy targets for Western companies seeking new markets.
Cook regularly accused the outgoing Conservative government of closing their eyes when it came to approving the export of arms and defence equipment to countries with imperfect human rights records.
Although commentators across the British political spectrum agreed Cook's intentions were noble, they wondered whether he had in fact achieved anything more than fashion a rod for his own back.

"Plainly, by the Cook test, all customers for British arms should pass a human rights threshold, encompassing not only democracy but freedom from repression. Many buyers -- Saudi Arabia, Indonesia -- do not survive even mild scrutiny of these matters," wrote Hugo Young of the liberal-minded Guardian newspaper.
In the mid-1980s Saudi Arabia awarded Britain two oil-for-arms deals worth 20 billion pounds ($32 billion) in one of the largest weapons sales in history.

"The Saudi deal has become essential for companies like Vickers, Rolls-Royce and British Aerospace...(it) is one of the major reasons why Britain is the world's second biggest exporter of arms," said the right-wing Daily Telegraph newspaper.
"Robin Cook would be utterly mad to put that kind of business at risk, and he will not."
EU CODE OF CONDUCT SOUGHT
Cook said Britain would look much more closely at firms seeking export licences to sell arms to sensitive states.
He also wants a European Union code of conduct to ensure that, if Britain refused to sell arms to a certain country, other EU members would not step in and pick up the contracts.
But Dr John Casey, historian and fellow of Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, dismissed this as futile posturing.

"Those countries will award their contacts elsewhere. States which bomb their rebellious minorities, or imprison or torture people for their religious or political beliefs, will not have the slightest difficulty in getting arms," he said.

"An ill-judged word from the foreign secretary, a sudden fit of morality offensive to a touchy foreign government, could cost thousands of jobs in the defence industry -- many of them those of Labour voters," he wrote in the Daily Mail.

Right-wing columnist Anne Applebaum said Cook should take heed of what happened to former U.S. president Jimmy Carter, who tried to bring morality back to foreign politics but was beset by a series of disasters which made him look weak.
"Christian piety, good though it is in individuals, is not for governments, British or American," she wrote in the Evening Standard newspaper.
CLINTON ON CHINA: REALITY BEATS MORALITY
Perhaps the best example of reality vanquishing morality was President Bill Clinton's decision in May 1994 to sever the link between human rights in China and trade.

Clinton put on a brave face, saying he preferred the idea of constructive engagement to try to change China gradually, but few forgot how he had attacked former president George Bush for "mollycoddling dictators" in the 1992 election race.
Clinton's decision helped U.S. firms win billions of dollars in Chinese orders, but left human rights organsations seething over what they saw as his surrender to big business.
Influential House of Representatives leader Bill Paxon said this had yielded "a Chinese regime which thumbs its nose at the United States and places its heel on the neck of freedom".
His words will have rung a bell in Canada, where critics mauled Prime Minister Jean Chretien for allegedly selling his soul to industrial interests.

Before winning a 1994 election, Chretien talked tough on China but within three years he dropped plans to criticise Beijing for its human rights record, preferring instead to concentrate on a series of massive trade deals.
The lessons and pitfalls facing Cook are clear.
"There's no such thing as an ethical free ride. When the choice lies between principles and jobs, Mr Cook will need to be encouraged not to betray his principles," said Hugo Young.
AMNESTY WANTS SAME STANDARDS FOR ALL
Richard Bunting of Amnesty International welcomed what Cook had to say and called on the foreign secretary to apply the same standards for all countries.

"The devil will be in the details...even if rich and powerful nations like China and Indonesia violate human rights, we would like to see them treated the same way as smaller countries which are more easily criticised."
Bunting told Reuters Amnesty wanted the Foreign Office to revoke arms contracts which had already been signed with countries such as Indonesia, under fire for alleged human rights abuses.
"All our research shows the British people do not want to turn on their televisions to see British equipment being used to suppress protests and kill people," he said.
